extracted.intended_audience: marketing scholars, consumer researchers, product managers, and business leaders designing or studying AI-enabled consumer experiences
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and guidance for understanding, evaluating, and designing consumer experiences with AI across four experiential types (data-capture, classification, delegation, social), plus organizational and design recommendations and a research agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI capabilities (ecosystem)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI conceptualized as an ecosystem comprising three fundamental elements—data collection and storage, statistical and computational techniques, and output systems—that enable products and services to perform tasks on behalf of humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite framing (listening/data collection; predicting/statistical techniques; output/communication or action) to map where consumer experiences arise and where interventions (design, audits, regulation) should be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer experience dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer experience relates to the interactions between the consumer and the company during the customer journey and encompasses multiple dimensions: emotional, cognitive, behavioral, sensorial, and social.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating AI-enabled products/services, assess impacts across these five experiential dimensions rather than only utilitarian metrics (efficiency, accuracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-capture experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The listening capability enables AI systems to collect data about consumers and the environment; the data-capture experience is the experience of endowing individual data to AI (data shared, surrendered, or captured from consumers' 'shadows').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both benefits (personalized services, convenience, self-improvement opportunities) and costs (lack of transparency, perceived exploitation, loss of personal control). Consider modalities (intentional vs ambient collection), frequency (intermittent vs continuous), type of data (environmental vs self/biometric), and context (home vs public) when judging customer outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-capture psychological consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Data-capture can produce negative affect, demotivation, helplessness, moral outrage, and psychological reactance due to perceived loss of control and exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure consumer feelings of control, reactance, and trust; monitor for behaviors like device abandonment, sabotage, false data entry, or anti-surveillance adaptations. Use netnography and sentiment analysis to surface such responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-capture sociological narrative: surveillance society
rubrics_metrics.description: The surveillance society narrative links data capture to loss of personal control and the commodification of private experience, producing cultural-level distrust and resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In strategy and communication, recognize and address this narrative—companies should not 'push' private information boundaries without accounting for cultural resonance and legitimacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational learning for data-capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms should determine and enhance organizational awareness around sociological and psychological costs of data-capture (e.g., privacy asymmetry and exploitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use netnography, sentiment analysis, engagement with privacy scholars/activists, and cross-firm sharing of lessons. Adjust internal assumptions (e.g., privacy defaults) to reflect vulnerable groups' perspectives and sponsor research on surveillance-society effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience design for data-capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interventions to limit exploitation in data-capture experiences through choice architecture, defaults, personalization, consumer education, and clearer communication of data use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overwhelming consent flows; consider personalized defaults; use AI to implement consumers' stated preferences; present clear, contextual information (e.g., Google Home app example); and balance opt-in mechanisms with minimizing choice overload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and rights-based standards for data-capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory frameworks and proposed norms (e.g., GDPR, algorithm bill of rights) aim to give consumers rights such as the ability to opt into data collection and the right to know when algorithms make decisions and what factors are weighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems and processes to comply with existing regulations (GDPR) and anticipate rights-based transparency requirements (disclosure of algorithmic decision-making criteria). Treat these as minimum standards when evaluating consumer-facing AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification experience
rubrics_metrics.description: AI's predicting capability creates classification experiences: consumers perceive AI's personalized predictions as the result of being classified as a certain consumer type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether classification yields feelings of being understood (affirmation, group membership) or misunderstood (incorrect labels, stereotyping, discriminatory predictions). Consider both subjective fit and socio-structural stakes (access to resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification sociological narrative: unequal worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification links to an 'unequal worlds' narrative where algorithmic categorization can sustain or amplify social inequalities (e.g., racial or socio-economic discrimination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating classification systems, examine how classifications map onto historic inequalities and how they may differentially restrict access to resources for marginalized groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification psychological consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers may feel misunderstood when AI makes incorrect identity inferences or when AI uses social categories in ways perceived as discriminatory, leading to frustration, moral outrage, and reductions in self-efficacy among vulnerable groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor user reports of inaccurate categorizations, measure perceived fairness and threat to identity, and assess downstream effects on behavior and self-concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational learning for classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms must learn about specific biases in their algorithms and organizational processes—this requires cross-functional attention (not only data scientists) and proactive auditing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct audits for 'inaccurate, unfair, biased, or discriminatory decisions' (per Algorithmic Accountability Act proposals), collaborate with computer scientists, sociologists, psychologists, and share audit processes and outcomes with stakeholders and policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience design to reduce misunderstanding and discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Design classification experiences that minimize feelings of being misunderstood by diversifying content, introducing 'taste breakers,' asking users to validate inferences, and instituting anti-bias protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer mechanisms for user validation and updating of profiles, periodically solicit corrections, experiment with diversifying recommendations to avoid overfitting to past behavior, and design rapid-reaction protocols when audits uncover bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debiasing and audit protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular, technology-appropriate audits and protocols are required to detect and address discrimination embedded in AI systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute regular algorithmic audits, prepare swift remediation steps, engage external experts, and lobby for meaningful regulation that protects consumers without imposing impractical controls on firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify organizational composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversify hiring and internal representation (including social minority groups) to reduce blind spots that perpetuate biased algorithms and culturally narrow products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diverse teams to influence culture, data curation, feature selection, and evaluation metrics to mitigate built-in biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegation is the experience of engaging in production processes where AI performs tasks on behalf of the consumer; this experience can empower consumers (by reducing cognitive/effort costs) or replace them (threatening agency, identity, and status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which tasks are perceived as 'humanness'-laden or symbolic versus instrumental, assess consumer preferences for autonomy versus convenience, and design delegation boundaries and opt-outs accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation psychological and behavioral consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling replaced by AI can create aversion, identity threats, and compensatory behaviors (resistance to automation), especially in symbolic consumption contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure preferences for human vs. machine labor across contexts, monitor compensatory non-consumption or identity-affirming behaviors, and consider policies that preserve consumers' role in valued processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Social is the experience of interactive communication with an AI partner; this can connect consumers (companionship, assistance) or alienate/objectify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess anthropomorphism effects (can increase trust but may undermine autonomy), disclosure timing (when to disclose machine partner to avoid alienation), situational and cultural moderators, and the role of brand equity in reducing alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principles for social experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interactive AI to foster genuine connection without deception or objectification; consider disclosure, timing, situational cues, and design choices that influence perceived humanness and agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test different disclosure timings and interaction styles; evaluate whether companionship experiences are perceived as deceptive or alienating; design to support consumer autonomy and reduce objectification.

rubrics_metrics.name: User participation and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater user participation in algorithm implementation (e.g., validating inferences, updating preferences) increases satisfaction with decision-support systems and can reduce frustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodically offer consumers opportunities to correct or refine algorithmic inferences; design interfaces that make validation easy and low-cost to reduce mismatch and perceived misclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice architecture and defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: The way options are presented influences consumers' sense of control in data-capture and other AI experiences; default options reduce cognitive load but can be paternalistic if not personalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choice architecture to reduce overload (e.g., appropriate defaults), consider personalization of defaults to account for preference heterogeneity, and use AI to implement consumers' stated privacy/data preferences automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and transparency as experience-levers
rubrics_metrics.description: Active consumer education about the costs and benefits of AI-data practices and clear communication of stored data and reasons (e.g., improved app transparency) reduce perceived exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement clear in-app explanations, contextual nudges, and easy-to-find privacy summaries; combine transparency with actionable controls to improve perceived fairness and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research agenda and empirical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of specific research questions (organized by experience type and interrelationships) that identify moderators, mechanisms, and outcomes for how consumers experience AI (e.g., socio-economic status effects, frequency of data-capture, uniqueness vs belonging motives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed RQs (RQA1–RQA10, RQB1–RQB6, RQC1–RQC8, RQD1–RQD7, RQE1–RQE6, RQF1–RQF6) to structure empirical programs evaluating contextual, cultural, psychological, and behavioral determinants of the four experiences and their interrelations.
